title: BMK-1 provides a redundant sorting force for spindle bipolarity
abstract: The proper development of embryos depends on faithful meiotic chromosome segregation to produce gametes. Failure of proper chromosome segregation results in aneuploidy, or the state of having an irregular number of chromosomes in a cell, which has human health implications due to its potential in causing congenital abnormalities and miscarriages. Though centrosomes are normally involved in cell division, oocytes lack centrosomes and must thus carry out chromosome segregation with acentriolar processes. By using C. elegans to study oocyte meiosis, this research project seeks to understand the motor forces responsible for bipolar spindle organization. Dynein is a motor protein known to sort microtubules with its polar properties, and the depletion of dynein results in splayed spindle poles that are unable to fully join together. When a monopolar spindle is induced by the depletion of the kinesin protein KLP-18, further dynein depletions result in the complete dissolution of the monopole. Interestingly, the resulting individual chromosomes are able to proceed through anaphase without having to first line up in the typical metaphase plate of chromosome segregation. By then depleting the BMK-1 protein simultaneously with both KLP-18 and dynein, we have found that BMK-1 provides a redundant motor force responsible for this spindle reorganization, which is normally undetectable due to the major forces exerted by dynein and KLP-18. Therefore, our studies have furthered the understanding of acentriolar oocyte meiosis and of how multiple motors work synchronously to establish and maintain bipolarity in the absence of centrosomes.
